newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak opposition blasts new anti-subversion law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak opposition blasts new anti-subversion law.

text.p: A former Slovak prime minister attacked a re-worked draft anti-subversion law on Wednesday as aimed against the opposition, but government supporters insisted it met European legal standards.
The law, which borrows from communist-era legislation, has aroused strong opposition within Slovakia, which is seeking early NATO membership, and expressions of concern from Western governments.

The coalition of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar distributed a new version of the law on "protecting the republic" this week to parliamentary deputies after President Michal Kovac refused to sign legislation which parliament approved earlier this year.

But Jozef Moravcik, who was briefly prime minister in 1994, said the Meciar government had made only cosmetic changes. "Even when they claim the law now conforms to Western standards there is no basic change in this new draft," said Moravcik, a former Meciar ally who leads the opposition Democratic Union.
"The new version retains the previous catch-all articles which can be interpreted almost at will and could be easily abused," he said. "We remain strongly opposed to it."
The United States and the European Union have criticised the legislation, which is part of an amendment to the penal code, and other legislation drafted by the Meciar government.
Both have expressed concerns that Slovakia is foot-dragging on its commitment to democracy.
Kovac refused to sign the original law and returned it to parliament for revision. The coalition withdrew it from the agenda in October, saying it would prepare a new draft.

Under the previous version people could be punished for organising anti-government demonstrations or publishing "false information" abroad. Some of its wording is almost identical to anti-subversion laws scrapped after the 1989 fall of communism.

The new proposal, expected to be debated by parliament in December, replaces the phrase "organising public rallies" with "calling for mass riots" which, its authors say, conforms to European standards.
"This amendment does not steer away from the standards of European legal structures," Roman Hofbauer of Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) told Slovak radio on Tuesday.

"Many people hide behind European norms, but there is no norm relating to this," said Vitazoslav Moric of the far-right Slovak National Party (SNS), the junior coalition partner which initiated the law.

Analysts said originally that Meciar had allowed the law to go ahead only to win SNS support for a treaty with neighbouring Hungary, a prerequisite for Slovak ambitions to join the NATO defence alliance and the European Union.
Both organisations have made clear that would-be members from post-communist Europe must settle all disputes with neighbouring countries before having any hope of joining.
Moravcik, who replaced Meciar when he was forced from power for nine months in 1994, said the law also bore the fingerprints of Meciar and his HZDS.
